prime.problem: The field's vocabulary hides the mechanism: the same word means different things in different sources (batch, α, β, K, TPS, NVLink bandwidth), and a new term tells you nothing about whether it saves FLOPs or bytes. Without a sorting rule, 80 terms stay 80 isolated facts.
prime.fits: The reference card for the whole series. The overview and stack cards named the levers and layers; this card gives each word one sentence, one number from the running example (Llama-3.1-8B, BF16, one H100) and the card that teaches it.
expect: the most-confused pairs (TTFT vs TPOT, total vs active, TP vs DP)
prime.goal: Place any new term into model / machine / arranging and say whether it saves FLOPs or bytes, tell the confused pairs apart with a number, and catch an overloaded word before comparing two sources.

attend: For the terms you already half-know, which of the three groups (model, machine, arranging work) does each belong to, and does it save FLOPs or bytes?
Why does the card single out memory-bound vs compute-bound as the pair that matters most?
Why does GQA raise the number of 8k-token sequences that fit from 14 to 59, and what does MQA push it to?
When the Scaling Book says "batch" and Kiely says "batch", what is each counting, and when do the two agree?
Why can goodput be zero at a batch size where raw throughput is higher?

must: Every term names a model part, a machine part or a way of arranging work → arranging work (batching, caching, sharding, quantizing) exists to keep the machine busy → metrics (TTFT, TPOT, throughput) say whether the arranging worked → so a new word is understood once you know its group and whether it saves FLOPs or bytes

Operation intensity vs the chip's ops:byte (≈ 295 on an H100) → below it the reads finish last (memory-bound), above it the math does (compute-bound) → memory-bound work speeds up from fewer bytes or more batching, compute-bound from better tensor-core use → so classify first, tune second

TTFT is paid once (queue + prefill) and TPOT on every later token (one decode step) → for a 1,000-in / 200-out request, 16.2 ms vs 199 × 4.84 ms → TPOT is about 98% of the wait → decode work usually matters more than prefill work for long answers

Words and symbols are reused across sources (batch = tokens vs requests, α = ops:byte vs acceptance rate, NVLink 450 vs 900 GB/s) → comparing numbers without checking the meaning gives wrong ratios → check the definition before comparing
elevated: Total vs active parameters → memory follows total, FLOPs and per-token reads follow active → DeepSeek-V3 stores 671B but uses 37B per token (74 GFLOP/token, not 1,342) → MoE needs much more memory than its compute suggests
reference: the exact Kiely definitions and page numbers (Appendix A, pp. 211–229)
hardware specs: 132 SMs, 256 KB SMEM per SM, 50 MB L2, H200/B200 figures
the Scaling Book symbol table (B, T, S, D, F, L, V, N, K, H, C, W)

compress.prompt: Course-level compress: without looking, draw three boxes (model, machine, arranging work) with the metrics underneath, and drop ten terms into them. Mark each term F (saves FLOPs), B (saves bytes) or neither.
checklist: model: weights, attention, KV cache, MLP, MoE; machine: SM, tensor cores, HBM, NVLink
arranging: batching, continuous batching, prefix caching, paging, sharding, quantizing, speculation
metrics: TTFT, TPOT, throughput, goodput, percentiles
most serving tricks save bytes (GQA, FP8, quantized weights, paging) because decode is memory-bound
the dividing line: intensity vs ops:byte (≈ 295 on an H100)

retrieve.q: Explain goodput to someone who only knows throughput, using the card's 10 ms TPOT example, and say why a provider sells goodput rather than throughput.
answer: goodput counts only requests that meet their latency targets
under a 10 ms TPOT SLO: 12,050 tok/s at batch 120, but 0 at batch 443 even though raw throughput is higher there
requests that miss the SLO aren't a product anyone pays for

retrieve.q: Walk through why GQA shrinks the KV cache: what is shared, how the per-token bytes change from MHA to GQA-8 to MQA, and what that does to how many 8k sequences fit.
answer: several query heads share one key/value head
KV per token: 512 KiB (MHA) → 128 KiB (GQA-8) → 16 KiB (MQA)
fewer bytes per sequence → 14 → 59 → 476 sequences of 8k tokens fit
a bigger batch, and fewer KV bytes read per step

retrieve.q: Tensor parallel vs data parallel across 8 H100s: what does each buy and cost, and which would you choose for a latency-critical product vs a cost-critical one?
answer: TP splits one model copy: weight read per step 4,794 → 599 µs, so each request gets faster, but chips talk every layer
DP runs 8 whole copies: 8× the tokens at the same 4.8 ms step, with no talking and no single request faster
latency-critical → TP; cost/throughput-critical with a model that fits → DP

retrieve.q: A dashboard says a model runs at "50 TPS". Before comparing it with your number, which two meanings could it have, and what else would you check in the same breath?
answer: Kiely's TPS is per-user perceived speed; most dashboards mean total server throughput
check the batch meaning too: tokens per step vs requests
and the units: GB vs GiB differ by 7%

compare.q: The glossary gives TTFT, TPOT, goodput and percentiles one line each; the serving-metrics card measures them. What does a one-line definition miss that you need before setting an SLO?
answer: how the metrics interact: bigger batch raises throughput but lengthens TPOT
that averages hide the tail: P99, not P50, is what users notice
measured numbers include queueing and overhead that the floors leave out

compare.q: The glossary says B<sub>crit</sub> = β·α<sub>hbm</sub> and gives 240/295/120/3,840. What does the full card explain that turns those numbers into a decision about batch size?
answer: why a linear layer switches from memory- to compute-bound at that many tokens per step
why int8 weights with bf16 math halve it (β = ½)
why MoE multiplies it by E/k: each expert sees only part of the batch
below B<sub>crit</sub>, batching is nearly free; above it, each extra token costs math time

compare.q: The overview ranks levers by effect on $/token; the glossary sorts words by what they name. Take speculative decoding: how does each card describe it, and which description helps you decide whether to turn it on?
answer: glossary: an arranging technique that uses idle math, with α and expected tokens per pass
overview: a lever worth 2.2× at batch 1 but a 0.70× slowdown at batch 256
the overview's view decides; the glossary's formula explains why the result flips with batch

predict.q: Keep K = 4 drafted tokens but drop the acceptance rate α from 0.8 to 0.6. Before computing: does the expected number of tokens per verify pass fall a little or a lot from 3.36?
predict.answer: It falls a lot, to about 2.31: (1 − 0.6<sup>5</sup>) ÷ (1 − 0.6) = 0.922 ÷ 0.4 ≈ 2.31. The later drafted tokens only count if every earlier one was accepted, so a lower α cuts the tail of the chain hardest.

apply.task: Use the glossary as a calculator. (1) E2E latency for 1,000 tokens in and 500 out on the H100 floor, using TTFT 16.2 ms and TPOT 4.84 ms. (2) Expected tokens per verify pass for α = 0.6 and α = 0.8 at K = 4. (3) Label each of these as saving FLOPs, bytes or neither: GQA, FP8 KV, FlashAttention, prefix caching, continuous batching, tensor parallelism.
apply.done: (1) ≈ 2,431 ms; (2) ≈ 2.31 and 3.36; (3) GQA and FP8 KV save bytes; FlashAttention saves HBM traffic (bytes); prefix caching skips prefill (FLOPs and time); continuous batching and TP save neither directly but rearrange work (more users per weight read; less weight read per GPU).
apply.hint: E2E = TTFT + (n<sub>out</sub> − 1) × TPOT; tokens per pass = (1 − α<sup>K+1</sup>) ÷ (1 − α).

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how sharply α changes the tokens per pass?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why TPOT dominates a 200-token answer's wait?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: intensity → memory-bound, or memory-bound → which lever helps?
Which overloaded word (batch, α, β, K, TPS) would have tripped you before this card?
Which linked card will you open first to turn a one-line definition into a formula?
